noteRef.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specPoints.text: understand the sources, roles and effects of the following hormones: adrenaline, insulin, testosterone, progesterone and oestrogen

primer.text: You know hormones are blood-borne chemical messengers. This note profiles the five on the specification: adrenaline the emergency mobiliser, insulin the glucose balancer, and the three reproductive hormones testosterone, progesterone and oestrogen. For each, file three facts — source gland, role, and the effects it produces in target organs.

lessons.title: Adrenaline and insulin
lessons.opening: Adrenaline is the fight-or-flight hormone: danger triggers it, and it floods the body with preparations for movement — faster heart and breathing, redirected blood, widened muscle vessels, and stored glycogen broken into glucose. Insulin is its daily-life counterpart: the pancreas secretes it when glucose runs high, and muscles and liver stash the surplus as glycogen.
keyPoints: Adrenaline, produced in danger situations, readies the body for fight or flight.
Its effects include faster heart and breathing rates and blood flow redirected to muscles.
Adrenaline also widens muscle blood vessels and prompts stored glycogen to break into glucose.
Insulin from the pancreas lowers blood glucose when it climbs too high.
Muscles and liver take up the excess glucose and store it as glycogen until levels normalise.

low.restatement: Adrenaline mobilises: heart up, breath up, blood rerouted, glycogen split. Insulin stores: glucose taken in by liver and muscles, packed as glycogen.
low.analogy: Adrenaline rings the fire bell and opens every exit; insulin is the steward who calmly herds everyone back inside afterwards.
low.examPointer: For each hormone give source, role and effect — the table's three columns — never the role alone.

medium.restatement: Both hormones act by changing target-organ activity: adrenaline multiplies muscle fuel delivery for emergencies, while insulin closes the glucose loop that keeps concentration inside its narrow homeostatic band.
medium.analogy: One is an accelerator pressed to the floor; the other is the cruise control that quietly trims the speed back.
medium.examPointer: Insulin's story is a negative-feedback loop — detection by pancreas, secretion, uptake, normalisation, secretion stops. Recount it in that order.

check.stem: Which situations prompt adrenaline production?

options.text: Circumstances where the body could be facing danger
options.explanation: Danger triggers the fight-or-flight hormone.
Meals trigger insulin, not adrenaline.
Sleep is not the named trigger.

options.text: When blood glucose falls too low
options.explanation: Low glucose is not adrenaline's trigger here.

check.stem: Which effect list matches adrenaline?

options.text: Faster heart and breathing rates, blood redirected to muscles
options.explanation: Those prepare the body for sudden movement.
Adrenaline speeds the pulse; the rest is mismatched.
That is insulin's effect.
Adrenaline widens them to feed muscles.

check.stem: What does the liver do with the glucose adrenaline releases from glycogen?

options.text: It ships the glucose to active muscle cells for respiration
options.explanation: Released glucose is transported to working muscles.

options.text: It converts the glucose back to glycogen at once
options.explanation: That undoes the emergency mobilisation.

options.text: It excretes the glucose in urine
options.explanation: Excretion is not the pathway named.

options.text: It stores the glucose as fat permanently
options.explanation: The emergency route is respiration, not storage.

check.stem: Which gland detects high blood glucose and responds?

options.explanation: Pancreatic cells detect the rise and secrete insulin.
The pituitary handles ADH, FSH and LH.
The testes produce testosterone.
Sweat glands are exocrine cooling organs.

check.stem: How do muscles and liver respond once insulin arrives?

options.text: They take up glucose and store it as glycogen
options.explanation: Uptake and glycogen storage lower the blood level.

options.text: They release glucose into the blood
options.explanation: That would worsen the high level.
Respiration continues; storage is the adjustment.
Only the pancreas secretes insulin.

check.stem: Name the hormone that readies the body for fight or flight.
State the storage molecule that insulin builds and where it is kept.
check.modelAnswer: Glycogen, stored in the liver and muscles.

check.stem: Explain why blood glucose control counts as another example of homeostasis.
check.modelAnswer: Glucose concentration must stay inside a narrow band — too high and cells lose water by osmosis, too low and the brain starves of respiratory fuel — so a detection-and-correction loop (pancreas, insulin, uptake) holds the level steady, exactly like temperature or water control.

check.stem: A student finishes a sugary drink. Track the pancreatic response and the final storage location.
check.modelAnswer: Absorbed glucose pushes the blood level high; pancreatic cells detect it and secrete insulin; muscles and the liver take the glucose up and convert it to stored glycogen until the concentration returns to normal and insulin secretion stops.

lessons.title: Testosterone and progesterone
lessons.opening: Two more hormones, two different theatres. Testosterone comes from the male testes and builds the male reproductive system plus its secondary sexual characteristics — facial and underarm hair, a deepening voice, extra muscle mass. Progesterone comes from the ovaries and guards pregnancy: it maintains the uterine lining and blocks further ovulation.
keyPoints: Testosterone is produced in the male testes.
It drives growth of the male reproductive organs and the male secondary sexual characteristics.
Male characteristics named include facial or underarm hair, deeper voice and greater muscle mass.
Progesterone is produced in the female ovaries.
It holds the uterine lining in place through pregnancy while further ovulation is shut down.

low.restatement: Testes make testosterone (male development); ovaries make progesterone (pregnancy maintenance, ovulation blocked).
low.analogy: Testosterone is the builder of a second-stage renovation; progesterone is the caretaker who locks the doors once tenants move in.
low.examPointer: Attach the sex and the organ: testes-testosterone, ovaries-progesterone — source marks are free marks.

medium.restatement: Both are ovarian-or-testicular steroid messengers whose effects are sustained developmental or maintenance programmes rather than minute-to-minute adjustments.
medium.analogy: They are building codes, not traffic lights — long-term instructions shaping structure rather than daily traffic.
medium.examPointer: Progesterone's dual action earns two marks: maintains the lining AND prevents further ovulation.

check.stem: Where is testosterone produced?

options.explanation: The testes produce testosterone.
Ovaries produce progesterone and oestrogen.
The pancreas produces insulin.
The pituitary produces FSH and LH.

check.stem: Which changes does testosterone drive?

options.text: Male secondary sexual characteristics such as a deepening voice
options.explanation: Voice deepening is a named characteristic.
Those are female characteristics driven by oestrogen.
That is progesterone's role.

options.text: Widening of muscle blood vessels in emergencies
options.explanation: That is adrenaline's effect.

check.stem: What does progesterone prevent?

options.explanation: Progesterone blocks additional ovulation while lining is maintained.
FSH maturation is not the named block here.
Unrelated systems.
That is ADH's territory.

check.stem: During pregnancy, which hormone keeps the uterine lining intact?

options.explanation: Progesterone maintains the uterine lining during pregnancy.
Emergency mobiliser, not pregnancy hormone.
Male-development hormone.
Glucose regulator, not pregnancy hormone.

check.stem: Which pairing of source and hormone is correct?

options.explanation: Progesterone is produced in the female ovaries.
The testes make testosterone.
The pancreas makes insulin.
Oestrogen comes from the ovaries.

check.stem: State the source and one effect of testosterone.
check.modelAnswer: Made in the testes; it drives growth of the male reproductive organs plus male secondary sexual characteristics.

check.stem: State the two actions of progesterone.
check.modelAnswer: Holding the uterine lining steady through pregnancy while further ovulation is prevented.

check.stem: Explain why blocking further ovulation serves pregnancy.
check.modelAnswer: A developing pregnancy needs the maintained uterine lining to stay undisturbed; releasing another egg during that time would restart the cycle's hormonal swings and risk the existing pregnancy, so progesterone holds the lining and shuts the door on further ovulation.

check.stem: A teenage boy notices his voice deepening and facial hair appearing. Name the hormone and its gland, and classify the change.
check.modelAnswer: Testosterone, produced by the testes, is responsible — voice deepening and facial hair are secondary sexual characteristics developing under its stimulation.

lessons.title: Oestrogen and the hormone summary
lessons.opening: Oestrogen, from the ovaries, carries a double brief. It drives female secondary sexual characteristics — breast development, wider hips, pubic and underarm hair — and it regulates the menstrual cycle by stimulating repair of the uterus lining after menstruation while steering egg release through its influence on FSH and LH.
keyPoints: Oestrogen is produced by the female ovaries.
It develops female secondary sexual characteristics.
Named characteristics include breast development, wider hips and pubic or underarm hair.
It stimulates repair of the uterus lining after menstruation.
It steers egg release through its influence on other hormones, FSH and LH included.

low.restatement: Ovaries make oestrogen: it shapes female characteristics, rebuilds the lining each cycle, and steers egg release via FSH and LH.
low.analogy: Oestrogen is the renovation manager — redecorating the room (lining) while coordinating the delivery schedule (egg release).
low.examPointer: Quote both briefs in cycle questions: characteristic development AND cycle regulation — half answers lose half marks.

medium.restatement: Oestrogen's cycle role is coordination through influence: by acting on the pituitary hormones it times the repair-and-release sequence rather than doing either job directly.
medium.analogy: It is the conductor who cues the orchestra's sections, playing no instrument itself.
medium.examPointer: Remember the summary table's five rows — adrenaline, insulin, testosterone, progesterone, oestrogen — each with source, role, effect.

check.stem: Where is oestrogen produced?

options.explanation: The ovaries produce oestrogen.
The adrenal gland produces adrenaline.
The testes produce testosterone.
The liver stores glycogen here.

check.stem: Which list gives female secondary sexual characteristics driven by oestrogen?

options.text: Breast development, wider hips, pubic and underarm hair
options.explanation: Those are the named female characteristics.

options.text: Deepening voice and increased muscle mass
options.explanation: Those are male characteristics from testosterone.
That is an adrenaline effect.
Unrelated to oestrogen's brief.

check.stem: What does oestrogen stimulate after menstruation?

options.explanation: Oestrogen rebuilds and thickens the lining after menstruation.
Breakdown precedes menstruation; repair follows it.
Nothing is closed; the lining is rebuilt.
Unrelated hormone system.

check.stem: How does oestrogen influence egg release?

options.text: Through its influence on the pituitary hormones FSH and LH
options.explanation: Oestrogen steers ovulation indirectly through the pituitary hormones.

options.text: By physically pushing the egg out
options.explanation: Hormones signal; they do not push.
No such mechanism exists.

options.text: It has no role in egg release
options.explanation: Cycle regulation is half its brief.

check.stem: Which hormone row of the summary table pairs insulin with its source?

options.explanation: The pancreas is insulin's source.
The adrenal gland gives adrenaline.
The ovaries give oestrogen and progesterone.
The pituitary gives ADH, FSH and LH.

check.stem: State the source gland and the two briefs of oestrogen.
check.modelAnswer: Ovaries; it develops female secondary sexual characteristics and regulates the menstrual cycle.

check.stem: Name the two pituitary hormones oestrogen influences for egg release.
Explain why oestrogen's lining repair matters for a possible pregnancy.
check.modelAnswer: After menstruation the lining is thin and unable to host an embryo; oestrogen's repair and thickening rebuilds a nourishing bed, so if an egg is released and fertilised that cycle, the uterus is ready for implantation rather than shedding the attempt.

check.stem: Complete the five-row checklist: for each of adrenaline, insulin, testosterone, progesterone and oestrogen, give its source.
check.modelAnswer: Adrenaline — adrenal gland; insulin — pancreas; testosterone — testes; progesterone — ovaries; oestrogen — ovaries.

glossary.definition: The fight-or-flight hormone that speeds heart and breathing, reroutes blood and mobilises glucose in danger.
The pancreatic hormone that lowers blood glucose by driving uptake and glycogen storage.
A storage polymer of glucose kept in the liver and muscles.
The ovarian hormone developing female characteristics and steering the menstrual cycle.
